{{short description|Theorem on quadratic pairing functions}}
{{use dmy dates|date=August 2026}}

The '''Fueter–Pólya theorem''', first proved by [[Rudolf Fueter]] and [[George Pólya]], states that the only [[quadratic function|quadratic]] polynomial [[pairing function]]s are the Cantor [[polynomial]]s.

== Introduction ==
In 1878, [[Georg Cantor]] showed that the so-called Cantor polynomial{{sfn|Cantor|1878}}
: <math>P(x,y) := \frac{1}{2} ((x+y)^2+3x+y) = \frac{x^2 + 2xy+ 3x + y^2 + y}2 =
x + \frac{(x+y)(x+y+1)}2  = \binom{x}1 + \binom{x+y+1}{2}
 </math>

is a [[bijective]] mapping from <math>\N^2</math> to <math>\N</math>.
The polynomial given by swapping the variables is also a pairing function.

Fueter was investigating whether there are other quadratic polynomials with this property, and concluded that this is not the case assuming <math>P(0,0)=0</math>. He then wrote to Pólya, who showed the theorem does not require this condition.{{sfn|Fueter|Pólya|1923}}

=== Statement ===
If <math>P</math> is a real quadratic polynomial in two variables whose [[restriction (mathematics)|restriction]] to <math>\N^2</math> is a bijection from <math>\N^2</math> to <math>\N</math> then it is

: <math>P(x,y) := \frac{1}{2} ((x+y)^2+3x+y)</math>

or

:<math>P(x,y) := \frac{1}{2} ((y+x)^2+3y+x).</math>

=== Proof ===
The original proof is surprisingly difficult, using the [[Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem]] to prove the transcendence of
<math>e^a</math> for a nonzero algebraic number <math>a</math>.{{sfn|Smoryński|1991|loc=Chapters I.4–I.5: The Fueter–Pólya Theorem I/II}}
In 2002, M. A. Vsemirnov published an elementary proof of this result.{{sfn|Vsemirnov|2002}}

==Fueter–Pólya conjecture ==
The theorem states that the Cantor polynomial is the only ''quadratic'' pairing polynomial of <math>\N^2</math> and <math>\N</math>. The conjecture is that these are the only such pairing polynomials, of any degree.

== Higher dimensions ==

A generalization of the Cantor polynomial in higher dimensions is as follows:{{sfn|Chowla|1961}}
:<math>P_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \sum_{k=1}^n \binom{k-1+\sum_{j=1}^k x_j}{k} = x_1 + \binom{x_1+x_2+1}{2} + \cdots +\binom{x_1+\cdots +x_n+n-1}{n}</math>

The sum of these [[binomial coefficients]] yields a polynomial of degree <math>n</math> in <math>n</math> variables. This is just one of at least <math>(n-1)!</math> inequivalent packing polynomials for <math>n</math> dimensions.{{sfn|Sánchez Flores|1995}}
